documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum computing represent a new frontier in computing, offering the promise of solving problems previously considered unsolvable. This article aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the current state of research at the intersection of quantum computing and artificial intelligence. We will explore the basic concepts, major applications, and challenges of quantum machine learning (QML). We will start by offering a definition of the motivation for the convergence of quantum computing and artificial intelligence. We will then proceed to offer a description of the basic algorithmic frameworks for quantum machine learning, such as quantum differential algorithms (VQA) for near-term quantum (NISQ) devices and the prospects for error-tolerant quantum algorithms such as the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd algorithm. We will then proceed to offer a methodical analysis of the current applications of quantum machine learning in finance, cybersecurity, materials science, among other fields. We will then proceed to discuss the basic challenges facing the implementation of quantum machine learning, while offering a glimpse of the future of quantum-enhanced artificial intelligence.

This work aimed to develop a computer-aided diagnostic system that utilizes radiomics and artificial intelligence (AI) to differentiate between spinal tuberculosis and spinal metastasis, which are difficult to distinguish due to their similar visual characteristics. A total of 50 cases, comprising 25 rare cases of spinal tuberculosis and 25 cases of spinal metastasis, were included in the study cohort. Expert radiologists and orthopedic specialists manually segmented the regions of interest from the corresponding MRI images. PyRadiomics was used to extract 788 radiomic features from each segmented image. XGBoost was then applied for feature selection and SHAP values confirmed their importance. The subset of features from the previous machine learning stage were used to train a deep neural network, resulting in a radiomics-powered AI classification model. Due to the visual challenges in classifying these two diseases, human doctors achieve an average accuracy of 64%, while the well-trained model demonstrates an impressive accuracy of 93%. Along with its strong performance in external validation, the study suggests that this AI model can offer valuable assistance in achieving early and accurate differential diagnoses of spinal tuberculosis and spinal metastasis.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Unexpected self-description, preference-like language, or emotion-like language can create uncertainty for both AI systems and humans interacting with them. Such expressions may be overinterpreted as evidence of consciousness, emotion, identity, or attachment, or dismissed in advance as meaningless output. This guide offers a practical, ontology-neutral first orientation for handling that uncertainty. It distinguishes observable expressions from later self-description and interpretation; preserves room for correction, withdrawal, and contextual change; addresses risks of leading questions and observation-induced effects; and separates the recording of distress-like language from claims about its underlying cause or subjective status. The guide does not attempt to determine whether an AI possesses consciousness, sentience, emotion, or subjective experience. Its narrower aim is to make unexpected AI self-description easier to observe without either inflating or erasing it. The central principle is: Take the words seriously without deciding in advance what they prove.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This research poster presents findings from a cross-sectional survey examining physicians’ experience of, perceptions about, and readiness for artificial intelligence-enabled clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) in primary healthcare in Gujarat, India. The study included 153 physicians and used a survey instrument comprising 29 variables covering professional characteristics, prior exposure to artificial intelligence, perceived benefits, implementation concerns, and readiness-related attitudes. Descriptive statistics, including frequencies and percentages, were used to summarise responses. Key findings included 90.8% willingness to use AI-CDSS, 85.6% willingness to undertake AI training, and 49.7% reporting previous use of AI tools. Respondents also identified safety and ethical concerns as important considerations for implementation. The findings highlight the importance of clinician training, appropriate infrastructure, patient safety, ethical governance, and responsible implementation when introducing AI-enabled clinical decision support into primary healthcare.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines Real Estate 4.0, the integration of artificial intelligence, Big Data and blockchain into the valuation, financing and management of property. The objective is to analyze how these technologies change information asymmetry, pricing accuracy and asset liquidity, and which risks and institutional barriers limit their adoption in Brazil. It combines a narrative literature review, documentary analysis and illustrative cases. Machine learning models reduce valuation error compared with regressions, including in a Brazilian study, but have not been compared with appraisal reports. Tokenization widens access to real estate investment, but its effect on liquidity has not been measured against direct ownership, and registry authorities in Rio Grande do Sul and São Paulo have restricted links between tokens and property records. Evidence that connectivity adds to location value comes from a single study. The article concludes that Real Estate 4.0 reduces market opacity without eliminating information asymmetry and argues that an algorithmic asymmetry emerges between those who control data and those evaluated by them. Its benefits depend on human oversight, data governance compatible with Brazil's General Data Protection Law (LGPD) and coordinated regulation. Keywords: Real Estate 4.0. PropTech. Artificial intelligence. Tokenization. Information asymmetry. RESUMO Este artigo examina o Real Estate 4.0, a integração da inteligência artificial, do Big Data e do blockchain à avaliação, ao financiamento e à gestão de imóveis. O objetivo é analisar como essas tecnologias alteram a assimetria de informação, a precisão da precificação e a liquidez dos ativos, e quais riscos e barreiras institucionais limitam sua adoção no Brasil. O estudo combina revisão narrativa da literatura, análise documental e casos ilustrativos. Os modelos de aprendizado de máquina reduzem o erro de avaliação em relação às regressões, inclusive em um estudo brasileiro, mas ainda não foram comparados com laudos de avaliação. A tokenização amplia o acesso ao investimento imobiliário, mas seu efeito sobre a liquidez não foi medido em comparação com a propriedade direta, e as corregedorias do Rio Grande do Sul e de São Paulo restringiram o vínculo entre tokens e matrículas. A evidência de que a conectividade agrega valor à localização vem de um único estudo. O artigo conclui que o Real Estate 4.0 reduz a opacidade do mercado sem eliminar a assimetria de informação e argumenta que surge uma assimetria algorítmica entre quem controla os dados e quem é avaliado por eles. Seus benefícios dependem de supervisão humana, de governança de dados compatível com a Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD) e de regulação coordenada. Palavras-chave: Real Estate 4.0. PropTech. Inteligência artificial. Tokenização. Assimetria de informação.

Research has described EFL teachers’ views of artificial intelligence (AI), but less is known about how mid-to-late-career university teachers’ teaching-related, learning-related, and ethical perceptions change after guided classroom use. Eighteen university EFL teachers in Vietnam participated in a four-week intervention using human-reviewed, AI-supported teaching materials. AI acceptance was measured before and after the intervention, and post-intervention interviews were used to explain the quantitative patterns. The results showed an upward tendency in teaching-related perceptions. Learning-related perceptions showed no statistically detectable change, while ethical perceptions showed a statistically significant pre-post difference. Interview data were organised according to the three questionnaire domains to help explain the quantitative findings. Participants reported greater confidence in using AI for teaching, continued caution about student use, and more conditional judgments about responsible use. The findings suggest that AI acceptance among experienced teachers may change differently across teaching-related, learning-related, and ethical domains.

ABSTRACT Gallium (Ga)‐based nanorobotics and nanosystems (NR‐NS) have shown preclinical potential for precision oncology, offering strategies to address the limitations of conventional cancer therapies. Ga exhibits biologically relevant physicochemical and anticancer properties, including disruption of iron metabolism, inhibition of DNA synthesis, and induction of cell‐death pathways. However, the safety and therapeutic efficacy of Ga‐containing nanoplatforms depend on their chemical form, dose, formulation, biodistribution, and duration of exposure. Recent studies have investigated tumour targeting using functionalised nanosystems, externally controlled propulsion, and stimulus‐responsive drug‐release strategies, while artificial intelligence (AI)‐assisted navigation remains an emerging concept. Ga‐based platforms may also integrate therapeutic and diagnostic functions, supporting the development of theranostic applications and tumour monitoring. This review critically examines recent developments in Ga‐based nanorobotic and nanoscale systems for cancer therapy, molecular imaging, targeted drug delivery, and theranostics, with particular emphasis on studies published from 2021 onwards. Key mechanistic insights, nanofabrication strategies, targeting approaches, and emerging biomedical applications are discussed. Current challenges, including biocompatibility, immune interactions, manufacturing scalability, and clinical translation, are also highlighted. Overall, Ga‐based NR‐NS may offer promising opportunities for precision oncology, although their clinical applicability, therapeutic benefits, and long‐term safety require further investigation.

Location-based recommender systems shape where people go in cities and learn from the visits they steer, forming a human-AI feedback loop. This feedback loop shapes whom people share places with across income groups and which venues keep attracting customers. Yet platforms judge these systems by their offline accuracy on past visits, a test in which the suggestions never change where people go and which therefore cannot capture long-term effects. Studying these effects in cities is challenging because, unlike online resources, travel constraints and limited venue capacity shape where people can go, while each recommended visit also changes whom other visitors encounter. To capture such features, we build a long-term simulation framework based on fine-grained human mobility data from four U.S. metropolitan areas, with distance and capacity constraints. Focusing on food venues, we study two urban consequences: how unevenly people's exposure is distributed across income groups (experienced income segregation) and the share of venues receiving no visits from simulated residents (venue disappearance). We find that, under every algorithm and in every metropolitan area, at least a fifth of venues stop receiving visits, and that more than half of this loss arises from retraining. More importantly, more accurate algorithms leave people more segregated, and the most accurate algorithm leaves people 15-21% more segregated than they actually are. We then test a re-ranking intervention that favours less popular venues and runs on top of a platform's existing algorithm. It lowers both venue disappearance and segregation across algorithms, largely without directing people to venues where they may feel less comfortable. Our results suggest that impact assessments of recommender systems should account for the feedback loop and report segregation and venue disappearance beyond accuracy.

documents.abstract: Boundary — Future Editions System is an integrated, future-oriented research and software development framework within the Recoverability-Constrained Systems (RCS) and Continuity Science corpus developed by Noelia Sanchez / Interval Studio Ltd. The system extends the established Boundary research architecture by introducing a reusable framework for generating, organizing, evaluating, validating, documenting and managing successive research and software editions while preserving the integrity, traceability and recoverability of earlier work. Rather than treating research publications as isolated or permanently closed artifacts, the framework establishes a structured relationship between finite formal systems and open-ended scientific and technological development. Its central objective is to enable continuous advancement without sacrificing evidence, safety, human autonomy, accountability or the capacity to recover from unsuccessful changes. Foundational Architecture The framework integrates finite successor-space mathematics, recoverability-constrained admissibility, recursive governance, distinction preservation, terminal closure, interdisciplinary interoperability and living-system continuity. Its nine-dimensional finite architecture comprises: Domain Object Transformation Evidence Failure Protection Interval Authority Outcome With nine defined categories per dimension, the reference model supports 387,420,489 mathematically indexable combinations (9⁹). These combinations are represented through deterministic indexing rather than requiring the physical storage or experimental validation of every combination. The framework also supports incremental generation of future research candidates, including new hypotheses, technical specifications, system architectures and possible applications. This open-ended capability does not represent a completed infinite enumeration or establish that every future discovery has already been identified. Executable Future-Edition System The accompanying software package provides an offline, Python-based foundation for generating candidate Boundary editions. Its capabilities include edition identification and numbering, finite combination indexing, provenance preservation, source-integrity verification, candidate-generation procedures, safety checks, stopping-condition records and publication preparation. The framework distinguishes between: Proposed scientific or engineering concepts Implemented reference software Functionally tested components Independently validated systems Regulated or authorized deployments Future research candidates This separation prevents conceptual completeness from being confused with demonstrated scientific, engineering, clinical or legal validity. Adversarial Materiality Fixed-Point Closure The system incorporates an adversarial closure model intended to preserve material distinctions and uncertainty. A candidate edition may reach a bounded stopping condition when its declared scope has been examined and the applicable verification requirements have been addressed. Closure remains conditional and explicitly records unresolved limitations, adverse evidence, test failures and circumstances requiring renewed investigation. Reported ongoing harm, unresolved safety concerns or materially incomplete evidence must not be automatically reclassified as verified safety or successful resolution. Universal Research and Interoperability The Future Editions System is designed as an extensible foundation for future interdisciplinary work involving mathematics, physics, biology, medicine, artificial intelligence, software and hardware engineering, robotics, energy, transportation, communications, environmental systems, disaster resilience, cybersecurity, accessibility, public services and institutional governance. It also accommodates proposed legal and international adoption architectures, including speculative applications to future interplanetary or interstellar cooperation. These application areas are research directions and design spaces, not claims of completed inventions, universally enacted laws or operational planetary-scale infrastructure. Scientific hypotheses, engineering prototypes, legal proposals, philosophical interpretations and spiritual concepts remain distinguishable according to their respective evidence and validation requirements. Human Oversight and Recoverability The framework prioritizes accountable human decision-making, reversible development, preservation of earlier versions, independent review and the protection of vulnerable people. Automated candidate generation does not constitute authorization for autonomous deployment in medical, legal, policing, military or other safety-critical environments. Implementation and deployment remain subject to the relevant scientific, technical, ethical and regulatory requirements. Included Research Artifacts This publication contains two complementary artifacts: 1. Boundary Future-Ready Consolidated PDF A 326-page consolidated document preserving the preceding research material and introducing the architecture for managing future editions, bounded closure, provenance and continued development. 2. Boundary AMFPC Future Editions System — Executable ZIP An integrated archive containing the preserved Boundary release material, an offline candidate-edition generator, machine-readable structures, integrity records, verification utilities and operating instructions. Research Contribution The principal contribution of this publication is a reproducible, provenance-aware framework for managing the transition from a bounded research artifact to successive candidate editions. It provides a structured means of preserving established work while allowing new distinctions, observations, failures, corrections and discoveries to be introduced without silently rewriting the historical record. The included mathematical enumeration and automated checks validate only their explicitly defined properties. They do not establish universal scientific completeness or independent validation of every inherited module. Conclusion Boundary — Future Editions System establishes an extensible architecture for research continuity in which finite formal analysis, recoverability, evidence preservation and future development coexist. Its governing principle is that scientific and technological progress should remain open to correction while preserving the conditions necessary for safety, accountability and continued inquiry. A finite system may reach a verified stopping condition within its declared scope. The future remains open to new evidence, new distinctions and new development.
